# Introduction

## What is Imaclim?

**Imaclim** is a macroeconomic model designed to analyze the interactions between the economy, energy systems, and climate policies. It is widely used for:

- Evaluating the economic impacts of climate policies (e.g., carbon taxes)
- Simulating energy transitions
- Producing long-term economic projections under different scenarios

Imaclim is typically implemented in **Scilab**, an open-source numerical computing environment.

## What is Quarto?

**Quarto** is a modern, open-source scientific publishing system. Think of it as a powerful notebook that lets you:

- Write text (in Markdown) and code **in the same document**
- Produce outputs in multiple formats: **PDF**, **Word (.docx)**, **HTML**, and presentations
- Keep your analysis, results, and commentary all in one place

This tutorial will show you how to use Quarto to document your Imaclim runs, present results, and produce professional reports.

## Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure you have:

1. **Scilab** installed — [https://www.scilab.org](https://www.scilab.org)
2. **Quarto** installed — [https://quarto.org](https://quarto.org)
3. **R** or **Python** installed (for post-processing results and producing charts)
4. The **IMACLIM-Country** repository cloned locally from GitHub:
   [https://github.com/GaelleLeTreut/IMACLIM-Country/tree/SNBC3_run3_122025](https://github.com/GaelleLeTreut/IMACLIM-Country/tree/SNBC3_run3_122025)

> **Important:** This tutorial is based on the branch **SNBC3_run3_122025**. Make sure you are on this branch before proceeding.

## Key Documentation

Two essential references for understanding the model:

- **Gaëlle Le Treut's thesis** (most up-to-date summary of IMACLIM-S):
  [https://hal.science/tel-01707559](https://hal.science/tel-01707559)
- **IMACLIM equations reference document**:
  [https://www.centre-cired.fr/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/cired_wp_2020_85_le_treut.pdf](https://www.centre-cired.fr/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/cired_wp_2020_85_le_treut.pdf)

# Setting Up Your Project

## Repository Structure

Once cloned, the IMACLIM-Country repository is organised as follows:

```
IMACLIM-Country/
│
├── code/                        # Scilab scripts to run the model
│   ├── ImaclimS.sce             # Main entry point — run this to launch a simulation
│   ├── Macro_Framework.sce      # Macro variables framework
│   ├── outputs_full_template.sce # Saves output variables
│   └── Test_AllConfig/
│       ├── main.sce             # Creates dashboards with variants
│       ├── main1.sce            # Runs all variant simulations
│       ├── def_of_MacroIncFRA.sce  # Declares variants to test
│       └── Class_default_dashboard.sci
│
├── study_frames/                # All model input variables
│   └── study_frames_FRA2018/
│       ├── Dashboard_FRA2018.csv   # Main dashboard (entry point for variables)
│       ├── Country_Selection.csv   # Select which country to study
│       └── AMSrun3mixnote/         # Scenario-specific input matrices
│           ├── IOT_Qtities_AMSrun3mixnote_1.csv  # Inputs for 2030
│           ├── IOT_Qtities_AMSrun3mixnote_2.csv  # Inputs for 2040
│           └── IOT_Qtities_AMSrun3mixnote_3.csv  # Inputs for 2050
│
├── Library/
│   └── economic_equations.sci   # All model equations
│
└── outputs/                     # Results written here after each run
    └── AMSrun3mixnote/
        ├── FullTemplate_AMSrun3mixnote.csv  # All variables, all years
        └── Summary_AMSrun3mixnote.csv       # Key variables only
```

## Creating Your First Quarto Document

Create a new file called `imaclim_report.qmd`. The `.qmd` extension stands for **Quarto Markdown**. Every Quarto document starts with a **YAML header** (the block between the `---` lines) that controls the document's settings:

```yaml
---
title: "Imaclim Scenario Analysis"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
format:
  pdf:
    toc: true
  docx:
    toc: true
---
```

To **render** your document to PDF and Word, run this command in your terminal:

```bash
quarto render imaclim_report.qmd
```

# Understanding the Imaclim Model Structure

## Key Concepts

Before running scenarios, you should understand the three main components of Imaclim:

**1. Calibration**
The model is calibrated to a **base year** (2018 for France). This means all model parameters are set so that the model exactly reproduces observed economic data for that year. You can skip re-calibration on subsequent runs by setting `skip_calibration;True` in the dashboard — this saves significant computation time.

**2. Exogenous Variables**
These are variables that are set *outside* the model — typically projections about the future that you feed in. Examples include:

- Population growth and labour productivity
- Household saving rates (`VAR_saving`)
- Energy and world commodity prices
- Carbon tax settings

> **Note:** If a variable is not present in the resolution system, it is treated as exogenous by default.

**3. Scenarios**
A scenario defines a particular set of assumptions and policy choices. The main scenario used in this tutorial is `AMSrun3mixnote`. Variants are created by changing specific variables (e.g., household consumption in the aviation sector).

## The Dashboard

The **Dashboard** (`study_frames/study_frames_FRA2018/Dashboard_FRA2018.csv`) is the central control file for any simulation. It contains all the variables that drive the model. Here is an annotated excerpt of the most important variables:

```
/// Simulation ///
Scenario;AMSrun3mixnote       // Name of the scenario
Nb_Iter;3                     // Number of iterations (2018 to 2050)
skip_calibration;True         // Skip calibration to save time

/// Households ///
H_DISAGG;HH1                  // Number of household income groups (1–10 deciles)
VAR_saving;99                 // Variant on the household saving rate

/// Sector aggregation ///
AGG_type;AGG_23TME            // Use the 23-sector version of the model

/// Carbon tax ///
Carbone_ETS;False             // No ETS carbon pricing
ClosCarbRev;CstNetLend        // Carbon revenue recycling option

/// Productivity ///
Capital_Dynamics;%F           // No capital stock dynamics
Demographic_shift;True        // Productivity depends on demographics
Labour_product;True           // Productivity depends on active population

/// Energy & commodity prices ///
World_prices;True             // Import energy prices active (gas, oil...)

/// Variant simulations ///
study;SNBC3_RunChoices3       // RunChoice file used for variants
VAR_C_airtransp;              // Variant on aviation household consumption
```

## The Reference Scenario

The reference scenario (`ref`) is always your baseline. All other scenarios are **compared against it** to measure the impact of a policy.

# Running Your First Simulation

## Step 1 — Select the Country

If this is your first time using the model, open the file `study_frames/Country_Selection.csv` and uncomment the country you want to study:

```
// For a study on France:
Country;France;FRA2018
```

## Step 2 — Launch the Simulation

Open Scilab, navigate to the `code` folder, and run the main simulation file:

```scilab
cd('IMACLIM-Country\code')
clear
exec ImaclimS.sce
```

This launches a simulation using the dashboard at:
`study_frames/study_frames_FRA2018/Dashboard_FRA2018.csv`

Results are saved automatically to the `outputs/` folder.

## Step 3 — Explore the Results

Once the simulation finishes, two output files are available for the scenario `AMSrun3mixnote`:

| File | Content |
|------|---------|
| `outputs/AMSrun3mixnote/FullTemplate_AMSrun3mixnote.csv` | All variables, all years (2018–2050) |
| `outputs/AMSrun3mixnote/Summary_AMSrun3mixnote.csv` | Key variables only |
| `outputs/AMSrun3mixnote/Time_2030/ioQ-run_2030_AMSrun3mixnote.csv` | Input-output quantities for 2030 |

# Analysing an Economic Shock

One of Imaclim's core strengths is simulating the macroeconomic impact of a **shock** — a deliberate change to one or more input variables. This section walks through a concrete example: **analysing the macroeconomic impact of a −10% and −20% reduction in household consumption in the aviation sector.**

The aviation sector corresponds to row 19 of the household consumption vector: `Proj_Vol.C.val(19)`.

There are two ways to create a shock in Imaclim.

## Method 1 — Shock via the Dashboard (recommended)

This is the preferred method as it keeps everything traceable and reproducible.

### Step 1 — Declare the variants in the RunChoice file

Open `code/Test_AllConfig/SCNBC_RunChoice3.sce` and add the variant logic for your new variable:

```scilab
// Modify aviation household consumption (row 19 = aviation sector)
if Scenario == "AMSrun3mixnote"
    if VAR_C_airtransp == "ref"         // Reference case
        Proj_Vol.C.val(19) = Proj_Vol.C.val(19);

    elseif VAR_C_airtransp == "-10%"    // -10% aviation consumption
        Proj_Vol.C.val(19) = Proj_Vol.C.val(19) * 0.9;

    elseif VAR_C_airtransp == "-20%"    // -20% aviation consumption
        Proj_Vol.C.val(19) = Proj_Vol.C.val(19) * 0.8;
    end
end
```

### Step 2 — Register the variants to test

Open `code/Test_AllConfig/def_of_MacroIncFRA.sce` and add your variable:

```scilab
test_fra_macro.VAR_C_airtransp = ['ref', '-10%', '-20%'];
```

### Step 3 — Add the variable to the default dashboard class

Open `code/Test_AllConfig/Class_default_dashboard.sci` and declare the variable:

```scilab
default_dashboard = struct( ..
    'Carbone_ETS' , 'False', ..
    ...
    'VAR_C_airtransp', '');
```

### Step 4 — Add the variable to the main Dashboard CSV

Open `study_frames/study_frames_FRA2018/Dashboard_FRA2018.csv` and add:

```
VAR_C_airtransp;-20%
```

### Step 5 — Add the variable to the output template

Open `code/outputs_full_template.sce` so the variable is saved in results:

```scilab
["VAR_C_airtransp", VAR_C_airtransp];
```

### Step 6 — Generate the dashboards

```scilab
cd('IMACLIM-Country\code\Test_AllConfig')
exec main.sce
```

This creates an intermediate file `code/Test_AllConfig/dashboards.dat` containing one dashboard per variant. You can inspect them in Scilab:

```scilab
dashboards      // lists all dashboards
dashboards(1)   // shows the first dashboard — check your changes are there
```

### Step 7 — Run all variant simulations

```scilab
exec main1.sce
```

This runs each dashboard in turn and saves results for each variant in the `outputs/` folder.

## Method 2 — Manual Shock on Input Files

This method is quicker for one-off experiments but less traceable.

1. Go to `study_frames/study_frames_FRA2018/AMSrun3mixnote/`
2. Copy and rename the folder — e.g. `AMSrun3mixlow`
3. Rename **all files** inside the new folder to match the new scenario name (every filename must contain `AMSrun3mixlow`)
4. Open `IOT_Qtities_AMSrun3mixlow_1.csv` (projection for 2030) and manually edit cell **Y20** to reduce aviation consumption. Repeat for `_2` (2040) and `_3` (2050) if needed.
5. Update the main dashboard to point to the new scenario:
   ```
   Scenario;AMSrun3mixlow
   ```
6. Run the simulation:
   ```scilab
   clear
   exec ImaclimS.sce
   ```

## Analysing the Shock Results

Once the simulation is complete, compare the variant outputs against the reference:

| File | Use |
|------|-----|
| `outputs/AMSrun3mixnote/FullTemplate_AMSrun3mixnote.csv` | All variables before/after shock |
| `outputs/AMSrun3mixnote/Summary_AMSrun3mixnote.csv` | Key variables summary |
| `outputs/AMSrun3mixnote/Time_2050/ecoT-run_2050_AMSrun3mixnote.csv` | Agent net lending (deficit) for 2050 |

> **Tip:** `code/Macro_Framework.sce` is an important file for understanding how macro variables interact — refer to it when interpreting shock results.

# Analysing Results in Quarto

## Loading Results

Inside your `.qmd` file, you can load and process your Imaclim output directly. Here is an example using **R**:

```{{r}}
#| label: load-data
#| echo: true

# Load results from the reference scenario
results_ref <- read.csv("../outputs/results_ref.csv")

# Quick look at the data
head(results_ref)
```

Or using **Python**:

```{{python}}
#| label: load-data-python

import pandas as pd

results_ref = pd.read_csv("../outputs/results_ref.csv")
print(results_ref.head())
```

## Plotting GDP Over Time

A typical first plot is **GDP evolution** across time steps:

```{{r}}
#| label: fig-gdp
#| fig-cap: "GDP evolution under the reference scenario"

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(results_ref, aes(x = year, y = GDP)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2E75B6", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(color = "#2E75B6", size = 2.5) +
  labs(
    title = "GDP — Reference Scenario",
    x = "Year",
    y = "GDP (billion EUR, constant prices)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Comparing Scenarios

To compare the reference scenario with a carbon tax scenario, you can overlay the two:

```{{r}}
#| label: fig-scenario-comparison
#| fig-cap: "GDP comparison: Reference vs Carbon Tax"

results_carbon_tax <- read.csv("../outputs/results_carbon_tax.csv")

# Add a scenario label to each dataset
results_ref$scenario        <- "Reference"
results_carbon_tax$scenario <- "Carbon Tax"

# Combine
all_results <- rbind(results_ref, results_carbon_tax)

ggplot(all_results, aes(x = year, y = GDP, color = scenario)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Reference" = "#2E75B6",
                                "Carbon Tax" = "#E05C2A")) +
  labs(
    title = "GDP: Reference vs Carbon Tax Scenario",
    x = "Year",
    y = "GDP (billion EUR, constant prices)",
    color = "Scenario"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Writing Your Report

## Mixing Text and Results

One of Quarto's most powerful features is **inline code** — you can embed computed values directly in your text. For example:

```markdown
The GDP in the final year of the reference scenario is 
`r round(tail(results_ref$GDP, 1), 1)` billion EUR.
```

This will automatically insert the correct number when the document is rendered — no copy-pasting required.

## Cross-References

You can reference figures and tables automatically:

```markdown
As shown in @fig-gdp, the economy grows steadily 
under the reference scenario.
```

## Adding a Summary Table

```{{r}}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Key indicators — Reference Scenario"

library(knitr)

summary_table <- data.frame(
  Indicator = c("GDP (final year)", "CO2 emissions (final year)",
                "Household consumption", "Investment"),
  Value     = c("3,250 bn EUR", "320 MtCO2", "1,850 bn EUR", "620 bn EUR"),
  Unit      = c("constant 2019 EUR", "MtCO2eq", 
                "constant 2019 EUR", "constant 2019 EUR")
)

kable(summary_table)
```

# Rendering Your Document

## Render to Both PDF and Word

To render to both formats at once, simply run:

```bash
quarto render imaclim_report.qmd
```

Quarto will produce:

- `imaclim_report.pdf`
- `imaclim_report.docx`

## Render to a Specific Format Only

```bash
# PDF only
quarto render imaclim_report.qmd --to pdf

# Word only
quarto render imaclim_report.qmd --to docx
```

## Previewing While You Write

During drafting, use `quarto preview` to see a live-updating HTML version in your browser:

```bash
quarto preview imaclim_report.qmd
```

---

# Tips and Good Practices

## Keep Code and Documentation Together

The main advantage of Quarto is that your code, outputs, and commentary live in one file. If you re-run the model with updated data, simply re-render the document — all tables and figures update automatically.

## Use `echo: false` for Clean Reports

If you want to show results but hide the code in the final report:

```yaml
execute:
  echo: false
```

Or for a single chunk:

```{{r}}
#| echo: false
# This code runs but won't appear in the report
```

## Version Control

Put your `.qmd` files under **Git** version control. This lets you track changes to your analysis over time and collaborate with colleagues.

```bash
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial Imaclim Quarto tutorial"
```

# Next Steps

Now that you have a working Quarto setup for Imaclim, here are some things to explore next:

1. **Add more scenarios** — create a function that loops over all scenarios and produces a combined comparison figure automatically.
2. **Parameterize your document** — use Quarto parameters to run the same report template for different countries or time horizons.
3. **Publish online** — use `quarto publish` to share your report as a website via GitHub Pages or Quarto Pub.
4. **Automate the pipeline** — combine the Scilab run and the Quarto render in a single shell script so everything runs end-to-end with one command.
